doc.title: Joe Ascione interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 17, 2001

title: Following Buddy Rich, not a protege; good players copy, great players steal
summary: Gene Krupa was his idol, then Buddy Rich. At eighteen he helped load Rich's gear, absorbing his playing but not copying him.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: In some of your promo material I read it says you’re a protégé of Buddy Rich. Is that something that you would consider or is that something that people write, for something to write?

Here’s the true story. When I was a young boy Gene Krupa was my idol. I met him in 1971 when I was ten and then he died in ’73 and I was really sad, and then I heard Buddy Rich, one of my male cousins who played drums gave me a record, a 1959 recording, “The Driver” it was called. Mike Mainieri, first record. Selden Powell, Earl May, McKenna. And it was like what is this, two, three drummers? I couldn’t understand what was going on. My ear to the stereo. So he became my new guy. So then I got to hear him and meet him and things like that. When I was about eighteen a friend of mine and I, before I went to college, we started following his band around. And we would show up at gigs in the whole Northeast of America. And at one point he said, “Hey you guys here again?” But at the end of the night like you have all this gear here you’ve got to pack up so the guys in the band just want to go eat, get paid, get the hell out. So I helped him. You know, “Yeah, we’ll help you load the stuff on the bus.” The next night, “Hey, you guys—” “yeah, put it up there.” And I just night after night gravitated towards the drum. Next thing you know I’m setting up the drums, breaking down the drums, setting up the angles, the heights, and getting everything right. And of course I did that to absorb that musical experience. And I remember taking pictures of it at all different angles when I was really into it. It was a good role model at the time when I was in my teens. So it was a function of that, of absorbing he and his music and that intense ability he had on the instrument, and that’s what it was. That’s what it was. I never looked to copy him, but just to try, if it were possible, to absorb some of that presence or that energy and that ability, that type of thing. I think good players copy great players steal.
I want to think about that one for a minute.
Well you can think about it.

Yeah. You hear a lot of guys who sound exactly like this. They’re good players but they’re copying. They don’t come into their own voice. But I love, I mean I still take lessons, I go to hear everyone, and I’ll hear this Cuban guy do this and I’m like, I’m taking that. Or hear this guy, I’m talking— ooh check that out, what’s this, how’s that? And the drumming community is like that. We can sit down, check this riff out, this pattern, look at this. Bass players talk about the instrument, you know, a hundred twenty years old, check out the wood. Guitar players, they hide from the lick, they don’t want you to copy their stuff. So everybody’s got, you now, the proclivities of each musical © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-
family. But the drummers share. But yeah I think good players copy, great players steal. But I wasn’t a Buddy Rich protégé.
